transcript:
Meeting header:

[00:00] Maya Chen (Redwood AE): ok everyone, hi, thanks for joining. we're going to dig into prefix hashing and tenant isolation. recorded at 21:00 UTC, duration ~58 minutes. quick intros... 
[00:15] Priya Nair (Stonebridge): hey all, priya here, infra lead, we've been seeing weird cache collisions in our dev cluster, thought it's time to review strategy before rolling to prod. 
[00:28] Jonah Patel (Redwood SE): morning/afternoon; jonah from redwood se. quick note — i'll propose a few key patterns; we might run a sim later. 
[00:40] Liam O'Connor (Stonebridge ML): liam — we run multi-tenant chat endpoints, about 120 tenants, some heavy, some spiky. hit rates vary widely. 
[00:52] Sara Gomez (Stonebridge Sec): sara — security, will focus on isolation, encryption and audit logs. 

Summary: short — review of prefix hash namespace, collision mitigation, TTLs, consistent hashing, and safe key derivation for multi-tenant prefix caching. action items and follow-ups recorded.

Topics: cache key entropy, tenant namespacing, deterministic vs salted keys, TTL strategy, eviction, KV cache on GPU vs DRAM, batching side-effects, quantization artifacts, VPC/on-prem constraints.

[05:10] Jonah: first, quick recap: Redwood's prefix cache uses a key that's typically a function of (model_id, prompt_prefix_hash, tenant_id optional, truncation window). Many customers only include model_id+prefix which is slightly risky with multi-tenant. 
[05:35] Priya: right — we found two different tenants getting the same cached completion, looked like a collision but might also be shared model variant. 
[05:44] Maya: important to differentiate collision vs intentional shared cache. if tenants opt-in to share, that's different. 
[05:53] Liam: can you explain, jonah, how the prefix_hash is computed? we saw a 64-bit hash in the logs. 
[06:01] Jonah: sure — default is murmur3_64 over the prefix bytes then base36 encoding; we also include sequence length bucket. murmur3 is fast but collisions exist at 64-bit level, though rare; with high cardinality tenants and huge prefix diversity, birthday paradox matters. 
[06:22] Sara: birthday paradox? like when collisions are more likely than you expect. that was one of our security flags — how do we mitigate? 
[06:30] Jonah: mitigation options: increase entropy (switch to 128-bit hash e.g., xxh3_128 or sha256 truncated to 128), namespace with tenant_id before hashing, or prefix with HMAC using tenant-specific secret (salt). tradeoffs are CPU cost vs safety. 
[06:52] Priya: namespace before hashing — does that mean we put tenant_id||prefix then hash, or we keep tenant separate in the key? 
[06:58] Jonah: either works. best practice: include explicit tenant namespace in the key metadata (e.g., tenant:123:key:abcd) and still hash the combined string for fixed-length keys. That way accidental collisions across tenants are virtually impossible. 

[10:12] Liam: if we namespace, does that break shared-cache features for customers that intentionally want shared prefixes? 
[10:20] Maya: good call — we support opt-in shared namespaces. default is isolated tenant namespace, customers can request a shared namespace per app/deployment. 
[10:32] Priya: for us, default isolation is required. we do want to avoid adding a tenant id to every request if it increases header size/perf. any perf overhead? 
[10:42] Jonah: negligible; string concatenation and 128-bit hash add a few microseconds CPU cost; on the critical path for high QPS you might want to offload key hashing to a preprocessor or do it in a sidecar. For Redwood Dedicated we can do this inside the runtime with minimal impact, we benchmarked ~0.6ms added at 10k RPS in our early tests. 

[13:05] Priya: collision we're seeing was at 0.02% hit mismatch across tenants measured over 24h, seems small but unacceptable. do you have tooling to simulate collision rates? 
[13:18] Jonah: yes — that's the sim we'll run (jonah: action item) — run realistic prefix distributions + tenant counts; use current hashing config and then with 128-bit salted keys. expecting collision rates to drop orders of magnitude. 

[15:00] Liam: another question: key stability across model rollouts — if we roll a model from v1->v1a (quantized) should we change keyspace? 
[15:10] Jonah: we recommend including model_variant tag in key derivation. otherwise a new kernel/quantized variant could pull stale cached KV entries with incompatible KV cache layout — which could cause incorrect completions or KV cache misses. 
[15:25] Maya: short version, include model_id:variant:token_len_bucket:tenant_id in the hash input. 

[18:42] Sara: encryption and KMS — tenant namespacing plus salted HMAC with tenant secret implies we need per-tenant secrets. how do we manage that in private deployments? 
[18:52] Jonah: for Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) you can manage secrets in your KMS; we support HSM/KMS integrations. Keys don't leave customer's control and HMAC is computed locally. For Hosted, we can offer per-tenant derived keys using customer-managed key in KMS via envelope encryption. 

[21:10] Priya: eviction and TTL — some prefixes are short lived, some are evergreen (system prompts). how to set TTLs? 
[21:20] Jonah: mix of heuristics and telemetry; default TTLs: short prefix (<50 tokens) -> 5 minutes, mid -> 30 minutes, long/ evergreen -> 24h. But customers usually tune this. Also recommend LRU eviction on per-shard basis and TTL-based cold-start. 
[21:44] Priya: LRU at GPU-level KV cache — do you do per-GPU or global? we saw hotspots where tenant A dominates a GPU evicting tenant B entries. 
[21:55] Jonah: Good point — sharding strategy matters. Options: tenant-aware sharding (pin heavy tenants to dedicated shards), consistent hashing with bounded load, or weighted allocation. For Dedicated deployments we support tenant pinning and custom shard weights. 

[25:03] Liam: what about batching interactions — if we batch tenants together to fill GPU, do we risk cross-tenant leakage? 
[25:12] Jonah: batching on the compute path is orthogonal to KV cache keys. compute batching accepts mixed-tenant inputs but cache key scoping prevents sharing. However, batching increases prefix reuse probability which can be good for hit rates. Need to ensure privacy by not deriving keys that mix tenants. 

[27:48] Priya: quantization — does using int8 models affect cache compatibility? we've had a case where cached KV from fp16 model didn't map when we switched to int8. 
[27:59] Jonah: yes, quantization can change KV format. cache entries are not portable across quantization schemes; that's why model_variant is critical in key derivation. Also we persist a small variant fingerprint in metadata to refuse incompatible reuse. 

[30:15] Sara: audit logs and forensic — if a collision occurs, we need to trace back which tenants/keys were involved. do you log raw prefixes? that's sensitive. 
[30:25] Jonah: we log hashes and metadata (tenant_id, model_variant, prefix_length_bucket), not raw plaintext. For customers requiring deeper forensics, we support encrypted prefix logs that only customer can decrypt (stored in their KMS). 

[33:05] Priya: on-prem constraints — we can't always push updates to runtime quickly; what's the recommended safe default for older runtime versions? 
[33:15] Jonah: back-compat guidance: if runtime < X.Y, use explicit tenant namespace in keys (no HMAC) and conservative TTLs. We will provide a migration tool that re-hashes existing cache entries when you flip on a new hashing scheme to avoid mass invalidation. 

[36:40] Liam: metrics — what telemetry do you expose to help us detect collisions/hit anomalies? 
[36:48] Jonah: per-tenant hit rate, per-shard eviction rate, collisions detected (hash duplicate incidents), prefix-entropy histogram, top prefixes by tenant. We also offer sampling of raw prompts under an allowlist for debugging. 

[39:55] Priya: one of our constraints is strict PII handling — any chance cached prefixes include PII? we often have user content in prompts. 
[40:05] Maya: default redact-in-transit: customers can opt-in to prefix-normalization redaction; you can also not cache prompts containing detected PII. Redwood also supports deterministic redaction and storage of salted hashes only. 

[42:30] Sara: for SOC2, we need to show isolation; can you provide an architecture diagram and proof of tenant key separation? 
[42:40] Maya: yes we'll attach a security pack. action: maya to send SOC2/KMS docs. 

[45:00] Jonah: two architectural patterns for safety: 1) Namespaced keys + 128-bit hash; 2) HMAC with tenant secret + per-tenant keyspace token. Pattern 1 is lower CPU cost; pattern 2 provides cryptographic separation if tenant secrets are compromised — bad actors can't compute cross-tenant collisions. 

[47:22] Priya: what's the runtime CPU vs mem tradeoff for 128-bit hashing at 10k RPS? 
[47:30] Jonah: rough numbers: extra ~1-2% CPU, ~0 bytes extra mem per key since hash replaces previous 64-bit token, slightly larger storage if we base36 encode. For high QPS, we'd recommend a small pool of hashing workers or hardware accelerated hashing. 

[50:05] Liam: ok can we run a pilot? we want to see collision sim results + dedicated deployment benchmark with tenant pinning. 
[50:13] Maya: yes — plan: jonah runs collision sim and shares data; stonebridge provides traffic traces; we schedule dedicated benchmark week of 2025-08-18. 

[52:00] Priya: also add a security walkthrough for our auditors. 
[52:05] Maya: noted — security pack + walkthrough scheduled. 

Recap (end): 
- Keep default tenant isolation (namespace keys) and include model_variant in hash
- Run 48h collision simulation and share results (Jonah)
